5.3 — Into the Cave: Persistence & the HUD

You break the door, you walk in — and for the first time, your coins come with you. You built the object that survives a scene load on 2.7; today you prove it works, and then put the numbers where a player can see them instead of in the Console.

Search terms for this lesson“in unity how to keep an object between scenes, how to make a singleton with dontdestroyonload, how to load another scene, how to show health on a canvas”Full walkthrough
Break It Down~10 minFull walkthrough

The numbers the player earned should still be there after they walk through a cave mouth — and the player should finally be able to see them. The first half is already solved in this project; the second half has not been built at all.

First, before any code: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

  1. Notice that a scene load replaces your objects, not just your viewUnity destroys every GameObject in the old scene and builds the next one from its file, so the Player you were holding is gone and the Player that appears starts from whatever its prefab and its fields say. Nothing was lost and nothing was saved — the numbers were replaced.Read: the SceneManager.LoadScene(int) row of the quick reference.
  2. Sort the facts: this room, or this runPosition, facing and the animation controller are facts about this moment in this room and must reset — SceneSwitch.cs already restores them, which is why walking into a cave does not strand you. Coins, current health and the maximum are facts about this run and must survive.Read: SceneSwitch.cs, the one given script in the project that already saves and restores something across a load.
  3. Check the owner a scene load is not allowed to destroyThe StatManager you built on 2.7: a public static field holding the one instance, an Awake() that claims it and calls DontDestroyOnLoad(gameObject) on the first load, and an early-return guard that destroys the copy every later load brings with it.Read: 2.7 — Refactor Day: the singleton you wrote, and the DontDestroyOnLoad(gameObject) row of the quick reference.
  4. Know which method owns each numberChangeHealth() is the only way in or out of health, and it carries the 2.3 ceiling and the death rule; ChangeCoins() floors the count at zero; Die() resets health and halves the coins. Nothing else may write those fields.Read: the three methods in your own 2.7 StatManager.
  5. Put the numbers on screen, read from that ownerA Canvas and a Text (TMP) label in the scene the game begins in, and a small script that reads StatManager.original every frame and writes the strings into .text.Read: the TextMeshProUGUI.text property, and the Console readouts you have been watching all year.

The whole split falls along one line: what belongs to this room and what belongs to this run. The hard part is already built — the object the scene loader is not allowed to destroy — so today is about proving it works and then giving it a face.

The test: could you look this part up on its own, right now, in one search? "Keep my stats between scenes" cannot be looked up. "Do not destroy this object when a new scene loads" can — it is one row of the quick reference.

Your turn

The project already contains one thing that survives a scene load: SceneSwitch.cs remembers which scene you came from, in a static field. Why is that field allowed to be static when your coins are not — what is different about the two things being remembered?

Today's design keeps your numbers alive across a scene load, and that is all it keeps them across. Quit the game and they are gone — is that a hole in the design, or the design itself?

In the Editor ~30 min
  1. Game view → press Play from Start (index 0) and play for a minute: collect a few coins, take a spike hit. Then walk into one of the cave mouths. The numbers follow you now — the Console line is the same before and after. Notice what did not follow: your position, your facing, your animation controller. Those came back from somewhere else.
  2. File → Build Profiles → Scene List (older tutorials call this Build Settings): three scenes, and their order is the load index — Start (index 0), Overworld (index 1), Platformer (index 2). Start (index 0) is what a built game loads first, and it is one of the two scenes that contains a StatManager object.
  3. Hierarchy → Overworld → one of the two cave mouths → Inspector → Scene Switch → Scene: an int, holding 0 on one mouth and 2 on the other. That number is a position in that list, not a name: nothing checks that index 0 is still the scene you think it is.
  4. Hierarchy → the StatManager object in Start (index 0). Press Play and walk to another scene: this object's name now sits at the bottom of the Hierarchy under DontDestroyOnLoad, not under the scene you entered.
  5. Hierarchy (Start (index 0)) → GameObject → UI → Text - TextMeshPro: one menu item makes three objects — a Canvas, a Text (TMP) child, and an EventSystem, which the UI wants even when nothing on it is clickable.
  6. Inspector → Text (TMP) → RectTransform → anchor preset → top-left, with a small offset from the corner, so the numbers stay put when the window is resized — a centre-anchored label sits over the middle of the game.
  7. Once HudController.cs exists — Inspector → Canvas → Add Component → Hud Controller, then Hud Controller → Stats Text → drag the Text (TMP) object in. An empty slot is a null reference that nothing complains about until the line that reads it runs.
In the Code ~45 min
APIWhat it gives youWhat it costs
public static StatManager original; A field that belongs to the class, not to an object — reachable with no reference and no search, and untouched by a scene load. It starts as null, and nothing claims it for you.
void Awake() Unity's earliest hook: every Awake() in a scene finishes before the first Start() runs. Order between two objects' Awake() methods is still not promised.
DontDestroyOnLoad(gameObject) The object moves into a scene of its own that never unloads, so it survives every load from then on. It takes a whole GameObject, not a component.
Destroy(gameObject) Removes an object — how the newcomer copy takes itself out of the game. The removal is deferred to the end of the frame: a line running later in that same frame can still reach it.
SceneManager.LoadScene(int buildIndex) What SceneSwitch.cs calls at every cave mouth — the line that would destroy your stats if nothing were persistent. Hand it an int and it loads whatever scene sits at that position in the build list.
Architectural specification — read the owner before you add a face.
  • The owner. Which field is the only reason your numbers survive a load, and what exactly does static change about where it lives? Which hook claims it, and what does the other branch do with a second copy?
  • The seam. Which methods may write health and coins, and where does the ceiling live — at the call site, or inside the method that owns the number?
  • The screen. Where does the HUD live, and what would one that read from the player show after a scene change?
  • The view. What state does HudController own? If the answer is none, say what that buys you the first time a number changes.

Socratic: Three ways to make a number survive

All three are real Unity techniques. Compare what each one costs you:

ApproachHow it worksWhat it costs
A static field on its own Belongs to the class — destroying the objects does not touch it. No lifecycle: you cannot reset it cleanly, and in the editor it survives between Play sessions, so testing lies to you.
A persistent singleton object — this project One object registers as the instance and asks Unity not to destroy it. You must handle the second copy a scene load brings.
A ScriptableObject asset Lives in a project asset rather than in a scene, so no scene load can touch it. A new concept and one more asset to manage — and it survives Play sessions too, which is either the point or a nuisance.
  1. Your stats should reset when you start a new game, and survive a scene change. Which of the three can express both of those, and which one cannot express the first?
  2. Start (index 0) already contains its own StatManager object. If you walk back to it later, what will be there — and what happens if nothing stops it from registering itself a second time?
  3. Why can position not be handled this way? What is different about position that makes SceneSwitch.cs handle it instead?
In the CodeFull walkthrough

The question this answers“how do I keep my coins and my health when I change scenes?”

You are editing Assets/Scripts/StatManager.cs. You wrote this file on 2.7. Today you read it against the question it answers: which of these lines is what actually survives the scene load, and which one stops the second copy from overwriting your run?

Step 1The slot, and the object that claims it

The fields and Awake(). Everything that survives lives on this object.

// StatManager.cs — the fields, at the top of the class.
    public int health = 3;
    public int maxHealth = 3;
    public int coins;

    public static StatManager original;

// StatManager.cs — Awake(), which runs before any Start().
    void Awake()
    {
        if (original != null && original != this)
        {
            Destroy(gameObject);
            return;
        }

        original = this;

        // Optional: Keep this object alive when switching scenes
        DontDestroyOnLoad(gameObject);
    }
  1. 2Current health, public so every caller can read it and every method here can change it. It starts at 3 because a new run starts at three.
  2. 3The ceiling. It is a separate field from health on purpose: one is game state, the other is the designer's number.
  3. 4The coin count. Defaults to 0, which is the right starting value for a run.
  4. 6The line the whole lesson rests on. static means the field belongs to the class, and a scene load destroys objects, not classes. It starts as null.Every word is load-bearing. Drop static and the field becomes a fact about one object — and the object is exactly what the scene loader deletes. original is empty again the moment you walk through a cave mouth, and your coins with it.
  5. 9The earliest lifecycle hook: Unity finishes every Awake() in a scene before it runs the first Start(). That is what lets every other script assume the slot is already filled.
  6. 11The duplicate guard: is there already a manager, and is it somebody else? Walk back into a scene that contains its own StatManager and this is true.
  7. 13The newcomer deletes itself — component, fields and the fresh coins = 0 it was about to claim the slot with.This branch is not a textbook exercise in this project. Start (index 0) contains its own StatManager, and the cave mouths can take you back to it. Without this line the newcomer overwrites original with default fields, and your run is erased the instant the scene finishes loading.
  8. 14The line that makes the guard a guard. Destroy() is deferred to the end of the frame, so the code below would keep running — and the doomed copy would set original = this a moment before it vanished, leaving every later caller pointing at an object that no longer exists.Read the shape, not just the words: one branch ends in return;, and everything that claims the slot sits after it. That is an early exit — the same shape as the if that stops a dead player in 2.7, used here to keep one object from doing two contradictory things in one frame.
  9. 17The first manager to load claims the slot with itself.
  10. 19The comment that ships with the file — and the one word in it you should argue with. In this project it is not optional: it is the entire mechanism. Delete the call and the comment above becomes true, which is the bug.
  11. 20The one call in Unity that changes what a scene load is allowed to do: this whole object moves into a scene of its own that never unloads.gameObject, not this. DontDestroyOnLoad() takes whole objects, and a component cannot outlive the GameObject that carries it. Notice what is not happening: the numbers are not being saved anywhere. They simply live on an object the loader is no longer allowed to delete.

Step 2The three methods that own the numbers

Nothing outside this file may write these fields — every change goes through one of these.

// StatManager.cs — the methods, below Awake().
    public void ChangeHealth(int amount)
    {
        health = health + amount;
        if (health > maxHealth)
        {
            health = maxHealth;
        }
        print("Health: " + health);
        if (health <= 0)
        {
            Die();
        }
    }

    public void ChangeCoins(int amount)
    {
        coins = coins + amount;
        if (coins < 0)
        {
            coins = 0;
        }
        print("Coins: " + coins);
    }

    public void Die()
    {
        health = maxHealth;
        coins = coins / 2;
        print("You died. Coins: " + coins);
    }
  1. 2The one door to health. amount is signed: a negative hurts, a positive heals, and the caller chooses the sign.
  2. 4Apply the change. This is the line a spike, a potion and a fireball all end up at.
  3. 5The ceiling from 2.3, applied inside the method that can bypass it — so no future caller can overheal. (The 2.3 page let you choose between an if and Mathf.Clamp(); this project took the if.)
  4. 7Clamp down to the ceiling.
  5. 9The Console readout you have watched since 2.1. It sits after the clamp, so it reports the value the game will actually use — which is also why 3.4's fireball shows the drop and 2.3's potion shows the cap.This is the line the HUD is about to replace. The Console tells you the number; the HUD will tell the player. Same value, same source, one audience each — and because both read the field after the method has finished changing it, they can never disagree.
  6. 10The death rule: at or below zero, the run ends. Note the <= — the build checks at zero and below, so a hit that takes you exactly to zero still kills.
  7. 12The method below, which owns what death means.
  8. 16The one door to the coin count, same signed-amount shape.
  9. 19The floor: a debt cannot show on the HUD as a negative number.
  10. 23The same readout, for the same reason — and the same line the HUD will duplicate for the player.
  11. 26Death, as this game defines it. public because the method is a promise the rest of the game can call — though today the only caller is ChangeHealth(). That is not an accident: it is what lets a later refactor add a respawn without moving the rule.
  12. 28Back to full. The player does not move: this is a reset, not a respawn.
  13. 29Half the coins are lost — integer division, so an odd coin disappears. That is the cost of dying.
  14. 30A readout that makes the death visible in the Console, because nothing on screen shows it yet. The else of that sentence is the next lesson's work, not this one's.
Check your work: the finished filebuild it as you read — then open this to check every line

Compare against your own file. Two lines have to be exactly right: public static StatManager original; — static, so the scene loader cannot reach it — and the duplicate guard, whose return; is what keeps the doomed copy from claiming the slot on its way out. Everything else you should be able to explain line by line; if you cannot, that is the line to re-read.

// ------------------------------------------------------------------
//  REFERENCE FILE — Assets/Scripts/StatManager.cs
//  Written to be read, not pasted. Build it with the walkthrough
//  above, one step at a time, then open this and compare.
//  If it is sitting in your project unchanged, that is the thing
//  to go and do now — the walkthrough is still above you.
// ------------------------------------------------------------------
using UnityEngine;


public class StatManager : MonoBehaviour
{
    public int health = 3;

    public int maxHealth = 3;

    public int coins;

    public static StatManager original;

    void Awake()
    {
        if (original != null && original != this)
        {
            Destroy(gameObject);
            return;
        }

        original = this;

        // Optional: Keep this object alive when switching scenes
        DontDestroyOnLoad(gameObject);
    }

    // Keeps track of health and prints it.
    // The cap and the death rule live here so every caller obeys them.
    public void ChangeHealth(int amount)
    {
        health = health + amount;

        if (health > maxHealth)
        {
            health = maxHealth;
        }

        print("Health: " + health);

        if (health <= 0)
        {
            Die();
        }
    }

    // Keeps track of coins and prints it.
    public void ChangeCoins(int amount)
    {
        coins = coins + amount;

        if (coins < 0)
        {
            coins = 0;
        }

        print("Coins: " + coins);
    }

    // The MVP death rule: reset health and lose half the coins.
    // No scene reload or respawn yet; that comes in a later refactor.
    public void Die()
    {
        health = maxHealth;
        coins = coins / 2;
        print("You died. Coins: " + coins);
    }
}
Build Lab: The HUD, and Where the Game Begins ~20 min

One decision is left, and it is yours: which scene should the game actually begin in? A Canvas is not persistent — it exists only in the scene that contains it.

ApproachWhat you doWhat it costs
Move the Overworld's Canvas into Start (index 0) Drag the Canvas and its Text (TMP) child across, then repair whatever breaks. Less setup, but a Canvas carries its scene's wiring with it: any button or listener that pointed at an Overworld object comes across as Missing, and the thing it used to do quietly stops happening.
Leave it alone and build a fresh Canvas in Start (index 0) One menu item: GameObject ▸ UI ▸ Text - TextMeshPro. A second Canvas exists in the project, and the Overworld's still switches off when you leave it — harmlessly, because nothing is drawn on it. You break nothing you did not write.

Either is defensible. This lesson builds a fresh one, because that path leaves the wiring you inherited exactly as you found it. Whichever you choose, write down your reason before you start: the checkpoint asks you for it.

In the CodeFull walkthrough

The question this answers“how do I put my coins and my health on the screen?”

You are editing Assets/Scripts/HudController.cs. A new script, and the Canvas you need for it is already standing in Start (index 0) — that was the editor work above. The script itself is a handful of lines: a slot for the text, a guard, and one string built from the values on StatManager.original. Every line is given.

Step 1Give the script a slot for the text

Two lines above the method: one using and one field.

using TMPro;

    [SerializeField] private TextMeshProUGUI statsText;
  1. 1TextMeshPro's types live in a namespace called TMPro, and the UI package that ships them does not put them in scope for you. Without this line the compiler cannot find the type on the next line, and reports an error that reads like a typo.
  2. 3The text object, wired from the Inspector. One thing here is new: the type is not GameObject or Transform, it is the component — because the component is what owns the text property you are about to write to.A slot for the component, not for the object. You have held component references since 2.2, but always by looking them up at runtime with GetComponent<Rigidbody2D>(). This one is dragged in by hand, which is only possible because TextMeshProUGUI is a component type the Inspector can hold.

Step 2Read the numbers from the manager, and write them into the text

One method, Update(), and it takes a position on the design question this lesson asks out loud: read every frame, and do not get clever about it.

    void Update()
    {
        if (StatManager.original == null)
        {
            return;
        }

        string statsLine = "Health: " + StatManager.original.health
                         + " / " + StatManager.original.maxHealth;

        statsLine = statsLine + "   Coins: " + StatManager.original.coins;

        statsText.text = statsLine;
    }
  1. 1Every frame, like your movement and your enemy logic. A number can change at any moment — a coin is collected in a trigger callback, damage arrives from a fireball you never see coming — so a readout that is only correct sometimes is worse than no readout at all.The alternative is "only rewrite the text when a value changes", and here it costs more than it saves. You would keep the last three values as fields and compare them every frame — three extra fields, and three extra chances for one of them to go stale and freeze the label forever. Reading a value is a field lookup; the expensive part is building the string, which is exactly what you would be avoiding. At this scale the honest engineering answer is the simple one, and the moment it stops being true the fix is right here: remember the last values, and rebuild the string only when one of them moves.
  2. 3The guard — and here it genuinely earns its place. This script can run in a scene with no manager at all: the Overworld and the Platformer both contain a Player, and neither contains a StatManager. Press Play from either one and this method runs every frame with nothing to read.Without this line the Console fills with a NullReferenceException sixty times a second. That does not crash the game; it buries every other message you might need, which is worse. With the line, the label simply keeps whatever it last said. Neither is a fix — the real fix is that the game begins in Start (index 0) — but the guard turns a flood into a blank label, which is a failure you can see.
  3. 5Nothing to show, so show nothing. return leaves the method immediately — the same early-exit shape as the death rule in your 2.7 health method.
  4. 8Build the line. The left-hand side is a local — a string that exists for this frame only, which is correct: it is thrown away and rebuilt next frame anyway, and a field would just be a place for a stale one to hide.Every value comes from StatManager.original, not from the player. The manager is the only object that still has the numbers, and the only one that survived the scene change — which is why the HUD can be trusted at all. Read them off the player and you get a fresh copy of the player's starting values in every new scene, which is the bug this lesson is about.
  5. 9And the ceiling, so the label reads 2 / 3. Showing the maximum and not just the current health is a small design decision worth naming: a player can only judge "am I in trouble?" against what full looks like.
  6. 11Appending to the string you already built. Note the shape: assign back to the same name, because a string cannot be changed in place — this makes a new one and points the name at it.
  7. 13The write. statsText is the component you wired in the Inspector; .text is the property holding the characters on screen. Assign to it and the label changes on this frame.Nothing reads the text back, and nothing stores it. The label is a view of the numbers, not a copy of them — it holds no game state of its own. That is what makes it impossible for the HUD and the truth to disagree. The moment you cache a number in this script "to save time", you have built a second source of truth, and it will be the wrong one.
Check your work: the finished filebuild it as you read — then open this to check every line

Compare against your own file rather than copying it. Three things to check: the using TMPro; line is there, the string is built inside Update() rather than once in Start(), and every value is read from StatManager.original rather than from the player. Your label text, your placement and what you choose to display are yours — the shape is the slot, the guard, and the rebuild in Update().

// ------------------------------------------------------------------
//  REFERENCE FILE — Assets/Scripts/HudController.cs
//  Written to be read, not pasted. Build it with the walkthrough
//  above, one step at a time, then open this and compare.
//  If it is sitting in your project unchanged, that is the thing
//  to go and do now — the walkthrough is still above you.
// ------------------------------------------------------------------
using UnityEngine;
using TMPro;

// HudController.cs — the numbers, on screen. It owns no state at all: every
// value is read from the manager each frame and thrown away again.
public class HudController : MonoBehaviour
{
    [SerializeField] private TextMeshProUGUI statsText;

    void Update()
    {
        // No manager in this scene (you pressed Play in the Overworld)? There
        // is nothing to show and nothing to crash over.
        if (StatManager.original == null)
        {
            return;
        }

        string statsLine = "Health: " + StatManager.original.health
                         + " / " + StatManager.original.maxHealth;

        statsLine = statsLine + "   Coins: " + StatManager.original.coins;

        statsText.text = statsLine;
    }
}
